about.title: About Kula
content: In ancient times, the volcanic region in and around Kula was called Katakekaumene, meaning 'the burnt land.' This name describes the area's appearance, covered with black lava. Ancient writers such as Strabo, Vitruvius, Stephanus of Byzantium, and Eustathius mentioned this region in their works. However, the only writer to describe Katakekaumene in detail is Strabo.

Strabo specifies the length of the region as approximately 9 kilometers and its width as 7 kilometers. According to him, it is a barren land covered with black rocks and ash, unsuitable for anything but viticulture. Strabo states that this appearance was formed as a result of 'fire from underground coming to the surface.' He also explains that the hills rising next to each of the three pits, called 'bellows,' were formed by hot materials erupting from underground.

In the same work, Strabo also reports that Katakekaumene was frequently shaken by earthquakes. It is mentioned that the people around Philadelphia (Alaşehir) in particular were accustomed to constant earth tremors and built their houses accordingly. The great earthquake in 17 AD devastated not only Sardis (Sart) but also a large part of Western Anatolia. The Roman Emperor provided support for the reconstruction of the region's cities.
During the reign of the Roman Emperor Decius (249–251 AD), a clergyman named Pionius, who lived among the local people, interpreted Kula's burnt appearance as 'a warning from God to the faithless.'

The borders of Katakekaumene were defined as Kula and Esenyazı to the south, the Gediz River to the north, Gökçeören (Menye/Maionia) to the west, and Kollyda (İncesu/Gölde) to the east. The cities of Maionia and Kollyda in the region were located on the famous Royal Road, which started from Sardis (Sart) and extended to Susa, the capital of the Persian Empire.
In this area, there were also cities like Thermai Theseos (Şehitlioğlu), Tabala (Güvercinlik), and Satala (Sandal); and numerous small villages around Körez, Ayvatlar, Hamidiye, and Ayazören.
Byzantine Period

Between the 11th centuries, Kula was within the borders of the Opsikion Thema, one of the military and administrative regions of Byzantium. During the Byzantine period, the country was divided into provinces called 'themata' for defense purposes, each governed by commanders called 'strategoi.'

The historian Pachymeres writes that Kula was a fortress that frequently changed hands between the Byzantines and the Turks. The name 'Kula' is thought to come from the Turkish root for 'fortress' and that this name began to be used during the Byzantine period.
In 1306, Catalan soldiers under the command of Roger de Flor advanced from Alaşehir and captured Kula.
Turkish Period and the Germiyan Beylik

Kula's Turkish history became prominent during the Germiyan Beylik period. During the reign of Yakup Bey I (1300–1340), the Germiyanids became a powerful beylik in Western Anatolia; during the time of his son Mehmet Bey (1340–1361), Kula and Simav were recaptured by the Turks.
A stone foundation inscription from the period of Yakup Bey II contains the following words:
'My ancestor Mehmet Bey took Küldi (Kula) from the infidel, and my ancestor Mehmet Bey took Simav lake from the infidel. I have made it lawful for the remaining heirs and have endowed these.'

During the reign of Süleyman Şah (1361–1387), the Germiyan Beylik experienced its most powerful period. To establish kinship ties with the Ottomans, he married his daughter Devlet Hatun to Yıldırım Bayezid, the son of Sultan Murad I. As dowry, Kütahya, Tavşanlı, Simav, and Emet were given to the Ottomans. Süleyman Şah spent the last years of his life in Kula, made it the capital of the beylik, and was buried in the Gürhane Madrasa upon his death.

When Yıldırım Bayezid ascended to the throne, he completely incorporated the Germiyan Beylik into Ottoman territory. After the Battle of Ankara in 1402, Timur returned the administration of the beylik to the Germiyanids. However, in 1428, Yakup Bey II went to Edirne and bequeathed his beylik to the Ottoman Sultan Murad II, passing away the following year.
Ottoman and Republic Period
During the Ottoman period, Kula was administered as a kaza (district) attached to the Sanjak of Kütahya. In 1852, it was attached to the Sanjak of Saruhan.

After the First World War, following the signing of the Armistice of Mudros, Greek forces landed in İzmir on May 15, 1919, and began the occupation of Western Anatolia; they also occupied Kula on June 28, 1920. However, after the victory on August 30, 1922, Turkish cavalry under the command of Fahrettin Altay entered Kula on September 4, 1922, and liberated the city.

Today, Kula is a city that still preserves its volcanic heritage, historical layers, and cultural richness, acting as a gateway from the past to the present. The traces of ancient Katakekaumene still live on in the stones, streets, and volcanic hills of Kula.

narMotifi.title: Pomegranate Motif
content: Turkish houses are generally dominated by woodwork. The newel posts of the stairs and the ceiling centerpieces are all made of wood, depicting many different figures. The pomegranate motif is one of the most used figures. The pomegranate, symbolizing abundance, is an indispensable fruit in the courtyard of every Turkish house and is also used as an important symbol in woodwork. It is also known that pomegranates were used for other purposes in the Ottoman Empire. In some regions, young men would propose to the person they wanted to marry by offering a pomegranate. We can see this in a well-known folk song today:
poem: If only the one coming were my love,
If only there were a pomegranate in her hand,
If only we were in one shirt,

sofa.title: Sofa (Hayat)
content: The upper floor plan, often referred to as the main floor, consists of a sofa and the rooms around it. Depending on the position of the sofa, houses are classified as having an internal, external, or intermediate sofa. Another name for the sofa is 'hayat'. Generally, the 'hayat' overlooks the courtyard. One or two stairs lead up from the courtyard to the 'hayat'. In many houses, the 'hayat' is divided into two sections: a harem (private section for women) and a selamlık (public section for men) pavilion. In some houses, there are 40cm high platforms called 'seki' at the transition from the 'hayat' to these pavilions. These platforms serve to elevate the pavilions slightly. According to a common belief, these platforms also marked a boundary for servants, which they were forbidden to cross in the presence of the masters and mistresses of the house. Additionally, in some houses, the harem pavilion has two platforms, and the second platform is said to be the boundary for the bride. This is because the most beautiful corner of the harem pavilion, which overlooks the entire courtyard, is the mother-in-law's corner. It would be disrespectful for the new bride to come here.
